q-123363.problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)={{v16}}$ along the line segment from ${{A}}$ to ${{B}}.$
q-123363.solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from ${{A}}$ to ${{B}}.$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a={{v1}}$ and $b={{v0}}.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & ={{v1}}+t[({{v0}})-{{v1}}] \\  & ={{v1}}+{{v9}}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x={{x_coordinate}}$ and $y={{v9}}$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({{x_coordinate}})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({{v9}})j \\  & ={{v10}} \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & ={{v8}} \\  & ={{speed}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={{v16}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & ={{v2}} \\  & ={{v3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({{v3}})\cdot {{speed}}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={{factor}}{\int }_{0}^{1}({{v4}})\text{d}t \\  & ={{factor}}{[{{v5}}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & ={{factor}}(1+{{radical_upper}})-0 \\  & ={{v6}}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-123366.problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)={{v2}}$ along the line segment from ${{A}}$ to ${{B}}.$
q-123366.solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from ${{A}}$ to ${{B}}.$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=0$ and $b={{v0}}.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =0+t\,(b-0) \\  & =t\,(b) \\  & =t({{v0}}) \\  & ={{v1}}\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x={{v8}}$ and $y={{v9}}$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({{v8}})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({{v9}})j \\  & ={{v0}} \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & ={{v5}} \\  & ={{v6}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={{v2}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & ={{v3}} \\  & ={{v4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{{v4}}\cdot {{v6}}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={{v6}}{\int }_{0}^{1}{{v4}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{v6}}[{{primitive}}]_{0}^{1} \\  & ={{v6}}({{v7}}).\end{aligned}
$$

q-76564.problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)={{v16}}$ along the line segment from ${{A}}$ to ${{B}}.$
q-76564.solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from ${{A}}$ to ${{B}}.$

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a={{v2}}$ and $b={{v0}}.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =({{v2}})+t[{{v0}}-({{v2}})] \\  & =({{v2}})+t({{v3}}) \\  & =({{v11}})\,i+({{v12}})\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x={{v11}}$ and $y={{v12}}$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({{v11}})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({{v12}})j \\  & ={{v3}} \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & ={{v9}} \\  & ={{v10}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={{v16}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & ={{v4}} \\  & ={{v5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({{v5}})\cdot {{v10}}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={{v10}}{\int }_{0}^{1}({{v5}})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{v10}}{[{{v6}}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & ={{v10}}({{epcube}}+{{epquad}}+{{epconst}})-0 \\  & ={{v8}}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-76605.problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{C}{{v4}}\,\text{d}s$ along the line segment from ${{A}}$ to ${{B}}.$
q-76605.solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from ${{A}}$ to ${{B}}.$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a={{v1}}$ and $b={{v0}}.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =({{v1}})+t[{{v0}}-({{v1}})] \\  & =({{v1}})+t({{v3}}) \\  & =({{v14}})\,i+({{v13}})\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x={{v14}}$ and $y={{v13}}$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({{v14}})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({{v13}})j \\  & ={{v2}} \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & ={{v7}} \\  & ={{v8}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={{v4}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & ={{v5}} \\  & ={{v6}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{{v4}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{{v6}}\cdot {{v8}}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={{v8}}{\int }_{0}^{1}{{v6}}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u={{v10}},$ $\text{d}u={{v11}}\,\text{d}t$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{{v8}}{\int }_{0}^{1}{{v6}}\,\text{d}t & ={{v9}}{\int }_{0}^{{{v12}}}{sec}^{2}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & ={{v9}}\operatorname{tan}⁡u\,{|}_{0}^{{{v12}}} \\  & ={{v9}}(\operatorname{tan}⁡({{v11}})-\operatorname{tan}⁡(0)) \\  & ={{v9}}({{tan_hi}}-{{tan_lo}}) \\  & ={{sec_final}}\end{aligned}
$$

q-76650.problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{C}{{v3}}\,\text{d}s$ along the line segment from ${{A}}$ to ${{B}}.$
q-76650.solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from ${{A}}$ to ${{B}}.$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a={{avec}}$ and $b={{v0}}.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & ={{avec}}+t[{{v0}}-{{avec}}] \\  & ={{avec}}+t({{v1}}) \\  & ={{v11}}\,i+({{v10}})\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x={{v11}}$ and $y={{v10}}$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({{v11}})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({{v10}})j \\  & ={{v1}} \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & ={{v8}} \\  & ={{v9}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={{v3}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & ={{v4}} \\  & ={{v5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{e}^{xy}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{{v5}}\cdot {{v9}}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={{v9}}{\int }_{0}^{1}{{v5}}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u={{v6}},$ $\text{d}u=({{v7}})\,\text{d}t$ as follows:  

$$
\begin{aligned}{{v9}}{\int }_{0}^{1}{{v5}}\,\text{d}t & ={{v9}}{\int }_{{{exp_lo}}}^{{{exp_hi}}}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={{v9}}\,{e}^{u}\,{|}_{{{exp_lo}}}^{{{exp_hi}}} \\  & ={{v9}}({e}^{{{exp_hi}}}-{e}^{{{exp_lo}}}) \\  & ={{v9}}({{endpoint_difference}})\end{aligned}
$$
